questions.stemHtml: In this transamination reaction, which of the following are the products X and Y?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Aspartate, α-ketoglutarate

 

In this transamination reaction, oxaloacetate reacts with glutamate to form aspartate and α-ketoglutarate. The transfer of an amino group from glutamate to oxaloacetate results in the conversion of oxaloacetate into aspartate, while glutamate is converted into α-ketoglutarate. This reaction is an important part of amino acid metabolism and the interconversion between the Krebs cycle and the urea cycle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alanine, α-ketoglutarate: Alanine is not produced from oxaloacetate in this reaction. Instead, oxaloacetate is converted into aspartate through the transamination process.

 

Option C. Glutamate, alanine: Glutamate is the amino donor in this reaction and is converted to α-ketoglutarate, not the final product. Alanine is also not involved in this particular transamination reaction.

 

Option D. Pyruvate, aspartate: Pyruvate is not involved in this reaction. The correct products are aspartate and α-ketoglutarate.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Oxaloacetate is converted to aspartate in a transamination reaction, with glutamate being converted into α-ketoglutarate.

questions.stem: Ingestion of benzoic acid in man results in an increase in urinary?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Hippuric acid

 

When benzoic acid is ingested, it binds with glycine in the liver to form hippuric acid, which is then excreted in the urine. This detoxification process helps eliminate benzoic acid from the body. Glycine plays a key role in this detoxification mechanism, allowing benzoic acid to be removed in the form of hippuric acid.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Phenyl pyruvic acid: This compound is a metabolite of phenylalanine, typically associated with phenylketonuria, but it is not related to benzoic acid metabolism.

 

Option C. Phenylalanine: Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid and does not play a role in the detoxification of benzoic acid.

 

Option D. Noradrenaline: Noradrenaline is a neurotransmitter and hormone, unrelated to the metabolic process involving benzoic acid and its urinary excretion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ingestion of benzoic acid results in the excretion of hippuric acid in the urine as part of the body's detoxification process.

questions.stem: Indole ring is present in?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Tryptophan

 

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that contains an indole ring in its structure. The indole ring is a bicyclic structure consisting of a six-membered benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. This indole ring gives tryptophan its unique properties, including its role as a precursor for serotonin.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Valine: Valine is a branched-chain amino acid and does not contain an indole ring. It has an aliphatic side chain.

 

Option C. Methionine: Methionine is a sulfur-containing amino acid, and its structure does not include an indole ring. It contains a methyl thioether group instead.

 

Option D. Histidine: Histidine contains an imidazole ring, not an indole ring. The imidazole ring in histidine plays a significant role in enzyme active sites but is chemically distinct from the indole ring.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The indole ring is specifically present in tryptophan, and it is a defining feature of this amino acid.

questions.stem: Which of the following amino acid will migrate slowest to the anode end at Physiological pH?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lysine

 

At physiological pH (around 7.4), lysine is positively charged due to the presence of an amino group in its side chain. The anode is positively charged, so lysine, which carries a positive charge, will migrate the slowest toward the anode because like charges repel. This results in lysine moving more slowly compared to other amino acids that are neutral or negatively charged at physiological pH.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aspartic acid: Aspartic acid has a negatively charged carboxyl group at physiological pH, which will cause it to migrate quickly toward the positively charged anode.

 

Option C. Glycine: Glycine is a neutral amino acid at physiological pH and will migrate toward the anode but at a moderate rate compared to charged amino acids like aspartic acid.

 

Option D. Valine: Valine is also a neutral amino acid at physiological pH and will migrate similarly to glycine but faster than lysine.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lysine migrates the slowest to the anode due to its positive charge at physiological pH.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements about protein structure is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Proteins consisting of one polypeptide can have quaternary structure.

options.label: B
options.text: The formation of a disulfide bond in a protein requires that the two participating cysteine residues be adjacent to each other in the primary sequence of the protein.

options.label: C
options.text: The stability of quaternary structure in proteins is mainly a result of covalent bonds among the subunits.

options.label: D
options.text: The information required for the correct folding of a protein is contained in the specific sequences of amino acids along the polypeptide chain.

questions.answerText: The information required for the correct folding of a protein is contained in the specific sequences of amino acids along the polypeptide chain.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) The information required for the correct folding of a protein is contained in the specific sequences of amino acids along the polypeptide chain.

 

The folding of a protein is determined by the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain. Certain amino acids like proline are never found in alpha helices due to their structural constraints, while glycine is usually not found in alpha helices either. In the case of collagen, glycine is present in every third position, forming a triple helical structure. Mutations in this sequence, particularly in glycine, can lead to conditions such as osteogenesis imperfecta, where the protein's folding is disrupted. Cysteine residues can form disulfide bonds that assist in the folding process, even when they are not adjacent in the primary sequence, as long as they are positioned correctly during the folding of the protein.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Proteins consisting of one polypeptide can have quaternary structure: This is incorrect. Proteins made up of only one polypeptide chain, such as myoglobin, do not exhibit quaternary structure. They can only achieve tertiary structure; as quaternary structure involves the interaction of multiple polypeptide chains.

 

Option B. The formation of a disulfide bond in a protein requires that the two participating cysteine residues be adjacent to each other in the primary sequence of the protein: This statement is false. Cysteine residues do not need to be adjacent to each other in the primary sequence to form disulfide bonds. They can be far apart in the sequence but come together during the folding of the protein to form the bond.

 

Option C. The stability of quaternary structure in proteins is mainly a result of covalent bonds among the subunits: This is incorrect. The stability of quaternary structure is primarily maintained by non-covalent interactions such as hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, and ionic bonds, rather than covalent bonds.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The specific sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain dictates how the protein will fold and function, and cysteine residues can form disulfide bonds even if they are not adjacent in the primary sequence.

questions.stem: Carbamoyl phosphate is involved in the synthesis of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Pyrimidine and urea

 

Carbamoyl phosphate plays a dual role in biological systems. It is an essential component in both the urea cycle and pyrimidine synthesis. In the urea cycle, carbamoyl phosphate combines with ornithine to form citrulline, a key step in detoxifying ammonia into urea. In pyrimidine synthesis, carbamoyl phosphate is used to form carbamoylaspartate, a precursor in the formation of pyrimidine nucleotides.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Purine and uric acid: Carbamoyl phosphate is not involved in purine or uric acid metabolism. These pathways are separate from those of the urea cycle and pyrimidine synthesis.

 

Option B. Purine and pyrimidine: Carbamoyl phosphate is involved in pyrimidine synthesis but not purine synthesis. Purine nucleotides are synthesized via a different pathway.

 

Option C. Purine and urea: While carbamoyl phosphate participates in the urea cycle, it is not involved in purine synthesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Carbamoyl phosphate is crucial for both pyrimidine synthesis and the urea cycle, but not for purine or uric acid metabolism.

questions.stem: Sulfhydryl group containing amino acid(s)?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cysteine

 

Cysteine contains a sulfhydryl group (-SH) in its side chain. This group is crucial for the formation of disulfide bonds, which help stabilize protein structures. The presence of the sulfhydryl group makes cysteine reactive, allowing it to participate in bonding that plays a critical role in protein folding and function.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Methionine: Methionine contains sulfur but lacks a sulfhydryl group. Instead, it contains a thioether group, which does not have the same reactivity as the -SH group in cysteine.

 

Option C. Serine: Serine does not contain a sulfhydryl group; it has a hydroxyl group (-OH) in its side chain.

 

Option D. Cystine: Cystine is formed from two cysteine molecules linked by a disulfide bond, and while it contains sulfur, it does not have a free sulfhydryl group.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The sulfhydryl group (-SH) is specifically found in cysteine, which allows it to form disulfide bonds essential for protein structure.

questions.stem: Tryptophan is?

options.label: A
options.text: Non polar, essential and pure glucogenic

options.label: B
options.text: Polar, essential and both glucogenic & ketogenic

options.label: D
options.text: Non polar, essential, both glucogenic & ketogenic

questions.answerText: Non polar, essential, both glucogenic & ketogenic
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Non polar, essential, both glucogenic & ketogenic

 

Tryptophan is a non-polar amino acid due to its large, bulky indole ring. It is classified as an essential amino acid, which means it cannot be synthesized by the body and must be obtained from the diet. Tryptophan is also both glucogenic and ketogenic, meaning it can be broken down to produce both glucose (glucogenic pathway) and ketone bodies (ketogenic pathway). This combination of features makes tryptophan a versatile and crucial amino acid in human metabolism.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Non polar, essential and pure glucogenic: Tryptophan is both glucogenic and ketogenic, not purely glucogenic.

 

Option B. Polar, essential and both glucogenic & ketogenic: Tryptophan is non-polar, not polar. It is classified as non-polar due to its indole ring structure.

 

Option C. Polar, non-essential, both glucogenic & ketogenic: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid, not non-essential, and it is non-polar, not polar.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tryptophan is a non-polar, essential amino acid that is both glucogenic and ketogenic, making it metabolically important for both glucose and ketone body production.

questions.stem: PKU is a congenital amino acid metabolic disorder. In one of the following rare variants of PKU, the enzyme deficient is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Dihydropterin Reductase

 

In some rare variants of PKU, the deficiency is in dihydropterin reductase, an enzyme necessary for the regeneration of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), a critical cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase. Without BH4, phenylalanine hydroxylase cannot properly function, leading to the accumulation of phenylalanine in the blood, similar to classical PKU. The absence of dihydropterin reductase affects the metabolism of phenylalanine and can lead to neurological issues if untreated.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Histidine decarboxylase: This enzyme converts histidine into histamine, which is unrelated to the metabolism of phenylalanine or PKU.

 

Option B. Phenylalanine Hydroxylase: While a deficiency in phenylalanine hydroxylase causes classical PKU, the question asks about a rare variant, where dihydropterin reductase is deficient.

 

Option D. Tyrosine Kinase: Tyrosine kinase is involved in phosphorylation reactions and is not related to the phenylalanine hydroxylase or tetrahydrobiopterin pathways in PKU.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In rare variants of PKU, the enzyme deficiency lies in dihydropterin reductase, leading to impaired regeneration of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), which is essential for phenylalanine hydroxylase activity.

questions.stem: Which of the following reactions occur both in mitochondria and cytosol?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Urea Cycle

 

The urea cycle involves steps that occur in both the mitochondria and the cytosol. Specifically, the first two steps of the urea cycle, including the formation of carbamoyl phosphate and citrulline, take place in the mitochondria. The rest of the cycle, which converts citrulline into argininosuccinate and finally urea, happens in the cytosol. A helpful mnemonic to remember processes occurring in both the mitochondria and cytosol is HUG: Heme synthesis, Urea cycle, and Gluconeogenesis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Glycolysis: Glycolysis occurs exclusively in the cytosol and does not involve the mitochondria.

 

Option C. Cholesterol Synthesis: Cholesterol synthesis takes place primarily in the cytosol and the endoplasmic reticulum, without involvement of the mitochondria.

 

Option D. TCA Cycle: The TCA cycle (Krebs cycle) takes place entirely within the mitochondria.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The urea cycle is unique in that it involves reactions both in the mitochondria and the cytosol, making it distinct from other processes like glycolysis and the TCA cycle​

questions.stem: Which of the following amino acid cannot participate in transamination:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Lysine

 

Lysine does not participate in transamination reactions. The amino acids that cannot undergo transamination include lysine, proline, and threonine. This is due to their structural properties, which prevent them from participating in the transamination process.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Alanine: Alanine can participate in transamination and acts as a substrate in these reactions.

 

Option B. Cysteine: Cysteine is also capable of undergoing transamination reactions.

 

Option C. Glutamate: Glutamate frequently participates in transamination reactions and plays a significant role as an amino group donor.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lysine, along with proline and threonine, cannot participate in transamination due to its structural properties.

questions.stem: A particular point mutation results in disruption of the α-helical structure in a segment of the mutant protein. The most likely change in the primary structure of the mutant protein is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Methionine to proline

 

Proline is never found in the α-helical structure because its rigid ring structure creates a kink in the helix, which disrupts its formation. Therefore, a mutation that introduces proline into a segment of a protein that normally forms an α-helix will prevent proper helix formation. A point mutation replacing methionine with proline in the primary structure would cause such disruption.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glutamate to aspartate: Both glutamate and aspartate are acidic amino acids with similar structures and properties, so this substitution would not significantly affect the α-helix.

 

Option B. Lysine to arginine: Both lysine and arginine are basic amino acids, and substituting one for the other is unlikely to disrupt the α-helix.

 

Option D. Valine to alanine: Both valine and alanine are non-polar, small amino acids, and this substitution would not likely affect the α-helical structure significantly.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Proline is not found in α-helical structures because it disrupts the helical conformation due to its rigid structure.

A point mutation replacing methionine with proline in the primary structure would cause such disruption. Other Options: Option A. questions.stem: A female neonate appeared healthy until age ~24 hours, when she became lethargic. A sepsis workup proved negative. At 56 hours, she started showing focal seizure activity. The plasma ammonia level was found to be 887 µmol/l (normal 5–35 µmol/l). Quantitative plasma amino acid levels revealed a marked elevation of citrulline but not argininosuccinate. Which one of the following enzymic activities is most likely to be deficient in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Argininosuccinate synthetase

 

Ammonia level was increased. Hyperammonemia was present. A marked elevation of citrulline was observed, while argininosuccinate was normal, which indicates the defect is at the point where citrulline is converted to argininosuccinate. The deficiency is in argininosuccinate synthetase.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Arginase: A deficiency in arginase would result in the accumulation of arginine, not citrulline.

 

Option B. Argininosuccinate lyase: A deficiency here would cause an accumulation of argininosuccinate, which is not seen in this case.

 

Option D. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I: A deficiency here would result in low citrulline levels, which is contrary to the elevated citrulline observed.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A deficiency in argininosuccinate synthetase results in elevated citrulline with normal argininosuccinate levels, causing hyperammonemia.

questions.stem: δ-Aminolevulinic acid synthase activity:

options.label: A
options.text: Catalyzes the committed step in porphyrin biosynthesis.

options.label: B
options.text: Is decreased in the liver in individuals treated with certain drugs such as the barbiturate phenobarbital.

questions.answerText: Catalyzes the committed step in porphyrin biosynthesis.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Catalyzes the committed step in porphyrin biosynthesis

 

δ-Aminolevulinic acid synthase catalyzes the committed step (rate-limiting step) in porphyrin biosynthesis. This first reaction in heme synthesis occurs in the mitochondria. The enzyme requires vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) as a cofactor, not tetrahydrobiopterin. It is also allosterically inhibited by heme, meaning that when there is a sufficient amount of heme, it will inhibit δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase. This enzyme's activity is increased, not decreased, in the liver when individuals are treated with drugs like phenobarbital, which induces the enzyme.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Is decreased in the liver in individuals treated with certain drugs such as the barbiturate phenobarbital: This is incorrect. Phenobarbital induces δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase activity rather than decreasing it.

 

Option C. Occurs in the cytosol: This is incorrect because δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase operates in the mitochondria, not the cytosol.

 

Option D. Requires tetrahydrobiopterin as a coenzyme: This is incorrect because the enzyme requires vitamin B6 (pyridoxal phosphate) as a coenzyme, not tetrahydrobiopterin.

 

Educational Objective:

 

δ-Aminolevulinic acid synthase catalyzes the first committed step in porphyrin biosynthesis and is the rate-limiting enzyme that requires vitamin B6 as a cofactor.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child was brought to his pediatrician for evaluation of gastrointestinal problems. The parents report that the boy has been listless for the last few weeks. Lab tests reveal a microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Blood lead levels are elevated. Which of the enzymes listed below is most likely to have higher-than-normal activity in the liver of this child?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) δ-Aminolevulinic acid synthase

 

In lead poisoning, enzymes such as ferrochelatase and porphobilinogen synthase (also called δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase) are inhibited. Lead poisoning results in decreased heme synthesis. When heme levels decrease, it removes the inhibition on δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase, causing its activity to increase. Therefore, δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase activity will be higher than normal in this patient.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Ferrochelatase: This enzyme is inhibited by lead poisoning.

 

Option C. Heme oxygenase: This enzyme is involved in the catabolism of heme, which is not directly related to the increase in δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase.

 

Option D. Porphobilinogen synthase: This enzyme is also inhibited in lead poisoning.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lead poisoning inhibits enzymes like ferrochelatase and porphobilinogen synthase, resulting in increased activity of δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase.



ore, δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase activity will be higher than normal in this patient. Other Options: Option B. Ferrochelatase: This enzyme is inhibited by lead poisoning. Option C. Heme oxygenase: This enzyme is involved in the catabolism of heme, which is not directly related to the increase in δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase. Option D. Porphobilinogen synthase: This enzyme is also inhibited in lead poisoning. Educational Objective: Lead poisoning inhibits enzymes like ferrochelatase and porphobilinogen synthase, resulting in increased activity of δ-aminolevulinic acid synthase.

questions.stem: A tRNA molecule that is supposed to carry cysteine (tRNAcys) is mischarged, so that it actually carries alanine (ala-tRNAcys). Assuming no correction occurs, what will be the fate of this alanine residue during protein synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: It will be incorporated into a protein in response to an alanine codon.

options.label: B
options.text: It will be incorporated into a protein in response to a cysteine codon.

options.label: C
options.text: It will remain attached to the tRNA. as it cannot be used for protein synthesis.

options.label: D
options.text: It will be chemically convened to cysteine by cellular-enzymes.

questions.answerText: It will be incorporated into a protein in response to a cysteine codon.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It will be incorporated into a protein in response to a cysteine codon.

 

When a tRNA is mischarged and carries alanine instead of cysteine, the tRNA will still recognize the cysteine codon. Since the anticodon of the tRNA determines the codon it binds to, this mischarged tRNA will incorporate alanine into the protein in response to a cysteine codon. The proofreading system that usually corrects such errors has not functioned, so the mischarged alanine will be incorporated at the position where cysteine should have been inserted.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It will be incorporated into a protein in response to an alanine codon: This is incorrect. The tRNA’s anticodon still matches the cysteine codon, not the alanine codon, so it will not respond to alanine codons.

 

Option C. It will remain attached to the tRNA, as it cannot be used for protein synthesis: This is incorrect because the tRNA will still participate in protein synthesis, and the alanine will be incorporated into the growing polypeptide.

 

Option D. It will be chemically converted to cysteine by cellular enzymes: This is incorrect. There is no enzymatic system that chemically converts alanine back to cysteine.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The fate of a mischarged tRNA is determined by its anticodon, meaning alanine will be incorporated into the protein at a position where cysteine is normally found.

questions.stem: Apo B48, B100 belongs to same RNA, difference between them is due to?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Differential RNA processing

 

The difference between Apo B48 and Apo B100 is due to differential RNA processing. This involves RNA editing, which alters the RNA transcript post-transcriptionally. Specifically, in the case of Apo B48 and Apo B100, the RNA is edited differently, leading to two different proteins from the same RNA. It is important to note that there is no role of splicing in this process, and the answer is differential RNA processing.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. mRNA splicing: This is incorrect because the difference between Apo B48 and B100 is not related to splicing.

 

Option B. Chemical changes in mRNA & splicing: While chemical changes in mRNA occur, splicing does not play a role in this specific case.

 

Option D. Different poly A tail: The poly A tail does not explain the difference between Apo B48 and B100.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The difference between Apo B48 and B100 is due to differential RNA processing, specifically RNA editing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely to be the recognition sequence for restriction endonuclease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) AATT

 

Restriction endonucleases recognize palindromic sequences, which means the sequence reads the same forwards and backwards. Out of the options provided, AATT is a palindrome and matches the recognition sequence for many restriction enzymes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Restriction endonucleases recognize palindromic sequences, and AATT is a common recognition sequence for these enzymes.

questions.stem: Number of high energy bonds required for the synthesis of Aminoacyl tRNA?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2

 

The synthesis of aminoacyl-tRNA, also known as the charging of tRNA, requires 2 ATP molecules. This energy is used to attach the correct amino acid to its corresponding tRNA molecule, and this process is catalyzed by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The synthesis of aminoacyl-tRNA requires 2 high-energy bonds in the form of ATP molecules.

questions.stem: Degeneracy of codons means?

options.label: A
options.text: More than one codon for a single amino

questions.answerText: More than one codon for a single amino
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) More than one codon for a single amino

 

Degeneracy of codons means more than one codon can code for a single amino acid. Degeneracy is responsible for silent mutations and is also related to the wobble hypothesis. The third nucleotide in the codon can vary without changing the amino acid being coded, leading to this concept of degeneracy in the genetic code.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Termination of protein synthesis: This is incorrect. Degeneracy refers to multiple codons coding for the same amino acid.

 

Option C. Transcription: This is incorrect. Transcription is the process of forming RNA from DNA, and is unrelated to codon degeneracy.

 

Option D. Translation: This is incorrect. Translation is the process of synthesizing proteins, while degeneracy refers to the redundancy of codons coding for amino acids.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Degeneracy of codons allows more than one codon to specify the same amino acid, contributing to genetic flexibility and silent mutations.

Option D. Translation: This is incorrect. Translation is the process of synthesizing proteins, while degeneracy refers to the redundancy of codons coding for amino acids. Educational Objective: Degeneracy of codons allows more than one codon to specify the same amino acid, contributing to genetic flexibility and silent mutations.

questions.stem: Met tRNA would recognize?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) AUG

 

Met-tRNA recognizes the codon AUG, which codes for methionine. This codon is the start codon used during the initiation of translation. Methionine is always the first amino acid incorporated into the protein chain in eukaryotic and prokaryotic organisms because of this initiation codon.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. GCA: This codon is not recognized by Met-tRNA, as it codes for alanine, not methionine.

 

Option C. GUA: This codon is incorrect as it codes for valine, not methionine.

 

Option D. UAC: This codon is incorrect because it codes for tyrosine, not methionine.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Met-tRNA specifically recognizes the AUG codon, which is the start codon for protein synthesis, coding for methionine.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the Wobble hypothesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Each amino acid is represented by only one codon

options.label: B
options.text: Base in third position of codon has reduced specificity for the same amino acid

options.label: C
options.text: Actively transported sugars are usually hexoses

options.label: D
options.text: Surface tension lowering substances get concentrated at interface

questions.answerText: Base in third position of codon has reduced specificity for the same amino acid
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Base in third position of codon has reduced specificity for the same amino acid

 

The Wobble hypothesis explains that the base at the third position of the codon has reduced specificity for the same amino acid, allowing some flexibility or "wobble" in base pairing. This means that the first two bases of the codon are more critical in specifying the amino acid, and the third base can vary without altering the amino acid being coded for. This flexibility is key to the degeneracy of the genetic code, where multiple codons can code for the same amino acid.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Each amino acid is represented by only one codon: This is incorrect as many amino acids are represented by more than one codon, which is a result of the wobble hypothesis.

 

Option C. Actively transported sugars are usually hexoses: This statement is unrelated to the Wobble hypothesis.

 

Option D. Surface tension lowering substances get concentrated at interface: This is unrelated to the Wobble hypothesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Wobble hypothesis refers to the reduced specificity of the third base of the codon, allowing flexibility in coding for the same amino acid.



ers to the reduced specificity of the third base of the codon, allowing flexibility in coding for the same amino acid.

questions.stem: Methylation of cytosine in gene causes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Gene silencing

 

Methylation of cytosine at the promoter region leads to gene silencing. When cytosine is methylated, it inhibits the expression of the gene, preventing transcription from occurring. This is a key mechanism in epigenetics, where changes in gene expression are not due to alterations in the DNA sequence but due to chemical modifications such as methylation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Increased replication: This is incorrect. Methylation of cytosine inhibits gene expression, not increasing replication.

 

Option C. Transcription activation: This is incorrect because methylation results in the silencing of the gene rather than its activation.

 

Option D. Histone acetylation: This is unrelated to the methylation of cytosine. Histone acetylation is a different mechanism involved in gene regulation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Methylation of cytosine at the promoter region results in gene silencing.

questions.stem: The hydrolytic step leading to the release of a polypeptide chain from a ribosome is catalyzed by which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Peptidyl transferase

 

Peptidyl transferase catalyzes the hydrolytic release of the polypeptide chain from the tRNA located at the P site of the ribosome. The release is triggered when a stop codon enters the A site, which is recognized by the release factors. Once the stop codon is recognized, peptidyl transferase performs the final cut, releasing the newly synthesized polypeptide chain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Dissociation of ribosomes: This occurs after the release of the polypeptide chain, not before.

 

Option C. Release factors: Release factors recognize the stop codon but do not directly catalyze the release of the polypeptide chain; they activate peptidyl transferase to perform this function.

 

Option D. Stop codons: Stop codons signal the end of translation, but the actual release of the polypeptide chain is carried out by peptidyl transferase.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Peptidyl transferase catalyzes the final release of the polypeptide chain from the ribosome at the P site, activated by recognition of the stop codon.

questions.stem: The ZYA region of the lac operon will be efficiently transcribed if:

options.label: C
options.text: The operator is mutated and can't be bound by the repressor.

options.label: D
options.text: The repressor is mutated and can't be bound by the inducer.

questions.answerText: The operator is mutated and can't be bound by the repressor.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) The operator is mutated and can't be bound by the repressor.

 

When the operator is mutated and cannot be bound by the repressor, the lac operon can be transcribed efficiently. In this case, RNA polymerase can bind to the promoter region, leading to the transcription of the ZYA region, which includes the genes for beta-galactosidase, permease, and transacetylase. The mutation prevents the repressor from inhibiting transcription, allowing the lac operon to be active regardless of lactose presence.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Glucose and lactose are available: The presence of glucose prevents the lac operon from being efficiently transcribed, as glucose inhibits the accumulation of cyclic AMP (cAMP), which is required for full operon activation in the presence of lactose.

 

Option B. cAMP levels are low: Low levels of cAMP indicate that glucose is present. Since glucose suppresses the activity of the lac operon, transcription of the ZYA region would not occur efficiently when cAMP levels are low.

 

Option D. The repressor is mutated and can't be bound by the inducer: If the repressor cannot bind the inducer (lactose), it will remain bound to the operator, blocking RNA polymerase from initiating transcription. Thus, transcription of the ZYA region will not occur efficiently.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Efficient transcription of the ZYA region occurs when the operator is mutated and unable to bind the repressor, allowing RNA polymerase to transcribe the genes necessary for lactose metabolism.

questions.stem: How do Di-Deoxy nucleotides inhibit DNA replication?

options.label: A
options.text: The analog becomes covalently bound to the enzyme and inhibits it

options.label: B
options.text: There is no 3’ Hydroxyl group to form the next phosphodiester bond

options.label: C
options.text: The analog can't form hydrogen bond to DNA template

options.label: D
options.text: Incorporation of the analog initiates rapid degradation of newly synthesized strand

questions.answerText: There is no 3’ Hydroxyl group to form the next phosphodiester bond
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) There is no 3’ Hydroxyl group to form the next phosphodiester bond.

 

Di-Deoxy nucleotides inhibit DNA replication because they lack the 3’ OH group. The absence of this group prevents the formation of the next phosphodiester bond, which is necessary for the continuation of the DNA chain. Without the 3’ hydroxyl, the DNA chain cannot be extended, leading to the termination of replication.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. The analog becomes covalently bound to the enzyme and inhibits it: This is incorrect because Di-Deoxy nucleotides do not inhibit DNA replication by binding to the enzyme but by preventing the extension of the DNA chain due to the lack of a 3' OH group.

 

Option C. The analog can't form hydrogen bond to DNA template: Di-Deoxy nucleotides can still base pair with the template strand; their inhibition of replication is due to the absence of the 3' OH group, not an inability to form hydrogen bonds.

 

Option D. Incorporation of the analog initiates rapid degradation of newly synthesized strand: The inhibition mechanism does not involve degradation of the DNA strand but rather the inability to continue synthesizing the strand due to the missing 3' OH group.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Di-Deoxy nucleotides inhibit DNA replication by preventing the formation of phosphodiester bonds due to the absence of a 3' OH group.

questions.stem: Restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis can only be used to follow the inheritance of a genetic disease if:

options.label: A
options.text: mRNA probe is used in combination with antibodies

options.label: B
options.text: The mutation is at or closely linked to restriction site

options.label: C
options.text: Mutation are outside of restriction sites so that cleaving still occurs

options.label: D
options.text: Restriction fragment remain the same size but their charge changes

questions.answerText: The mutation is at or closely linked to restriction site
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) The mutation is at or closely linked to restriction site

 

Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis can only track the inheritance of a genetic disease if the mutation is at or closely linked to the restriction site. The restriction endonucleases recognize and cut at specific palindromic sequences called restriction sites. If a mutation occurs at one of these sites or close enough to affect the restriction site, it changes the fragment sizes generated after digestion, which can then be detected and analyzed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. mRNA probe is used in combination with antibodies: RFLP analysis does not involve the use of mRNA probes or antibodies. It relies on DNA fragments created by restriction enzymes.

 

Option C. Mutation is outside of restriction sites so that cleaving still occurs: If a mutation occurs outside of the restriction site, it will not affect the cutting pattern of the restriction enzyme, making it undetectable by RFLP.

 

Option D. Restriction fragments remain the same size but their charge changes: RFLP analysis depends on the size changes of DNA fragments, not on charge differences. If the fragment sizes remain the same, no polymorphism will be detected.

 

Educational Objective:

 

RFLP can only detect genetic mutations if they occur at or closely linked to a restriction site, which alters the DNA fragment sizes after digestion.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl is brought by her parents to the dermatologist. She has many freckles on her face, neck, arms, and hands, and the parents report that she is unusually sensitive to sunlight. Two basal cell carcinomas are identified on her face. Based on the clinical picture, which of the following processes is most likely to be defective in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Repair of double-strand breaks by error-prone homologous recombination

options.label: B
options.text: Removal of mismatched bases from the 3′-end of Okazaki fragments by a methyl-directed process

options.label: C
options.text: Removal of pyrimidine dimers from DNA by nucleotide excision repair

options.label: D
options.text: Removal of uracil from DNA by base excision repair

questions.answerText: Removal of pyrimidine dimers from DNA by nucleotide excision repair
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Removal of pyrimidine dimers from DNA by nucleotide excision repair

 

The patient shows signs of sunlight sensitivity, freckling, and basal cell carcinoma, which are characteristic of a condition where the removal of pyrimidine dimers from DNA by nucleotide excision repair is defective. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight causes the formation of thymidine dimers (a type of pyrimidine dimer) in DNA. These dimers are normally repaired by the nucleotide excision repair mechanism. When this repair mechanism is defective, as seen in disorders such as xeroderma pigmentosum, the accumulation of thymidine dimers leads to DNA damage, resulting in skin abnormalities like basal cell carcinoma.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Repair of double-strand breaks by error-prone homologous recombination: This is incorrect as the clinical presentation points toward defective repair of UV-induced thymidine dimers, not double-strand break repair.

 

Option B. Removal of mismatched bases from the 3′-end of Okazaki fragments by a methyl-directed process: The patient's symptoms do not suggest a mismatch repair defect, but rather a defect in the nucleotide excision repair pathway for thymidine dimers caused by UV radiation.

 

Option D. Removal of uracil from DNA by base excision repair: Base excision repair is involved in the removal of uracil and other small, non-helix-distorting base lesions. This is not relevant to the patient's symptoms, which are related to UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The defect in the nucleotide excision repair mechanism leads to the accumulation of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, resulting in clinical features such as sunlight sensitivity and skin cancers.

questions.stem: In SCID, what type of DNA repair is defective:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Non-homologous end joining repair

 

In SCID (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency), the DNA repair mechanism that is defective is non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). This repair mechanism is essential for fixing double-strand breaks in DNA. In SCID, there is a defect in this process, leading to an inability to properly repair double-strand breaks, which are critical in the development of functional immune cells. This defect results in severe immunodeficiency, as the immune system cannot produce functional T and B cells due to failed DNA repair during recombination.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Base excision repair: Base excision repair is involved in fixing small, non-helix-distorting lesions in the DNA, such as deaminated cytosine. It is not the defective repair pathway in SCID.

 

Option B. Nucleotide excision repair: Nucleotide excision repair primarily fixes bulky DNA adducts, such as pyrimidine dimers caused by UV radiation, and is not related to SCID.

 

Option C. Mismatch Repair: Mismatch repair fixes errors that occur during DNA replication. A defect in this pathway leads to conditions like Lynch syndrome, but it is not implicated in SCID.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In SCID, the defective DNA repair mechanism is non-homologous end joining, which is essential for repairing double-strand breaks.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child who easily tires and has trouble walking is diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive disorder. Genetic analysis shows that the patient’s gene for the muscle protein dystrophin contains a mutation in its promoter region. Of the choices listed, which would be the most likely effect of this mutation?

options.label: A
options.text: Initiation of dystrophin transcription will be defective.

options.label: B
options.text: Capping of dystrophin messenger RNA will be defective.

options.label: C
options.text: Splicing of dystrophin messenger RNA will be defective.

options.label: D
options.text: Tailing of dystrophin messenger RNA will be defective.

questions.answerText: Initiation of dystrophin transcription will be defective.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Initiation of dystrophin transcription will be defective.

 

The gene for dystrophin contains a mutation in the promoter region. The promoter is the region where RNA polymerase binds to initiate transcription. A mutation in the promoter region would interfere with the binding of RNA polymerase, leading to defective initiation of dystrophin transcription.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Capping of dystrophin messenger RNA will be defective: This process happens after transcription has started, so a promoter mutation would not directly affect mRNA capping.

 

Option C. Splicing of dystrophin messenger RNA will be defective: Splicing is a post-transcriptional process and would not be affected by a promoter mutation.

 

Option D. Tailing of dystrophin messenger RNA will be defective: Tailing is also a post-transcriptional modification, so it would not be influenced by a mutation in the promoter region.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A mutation in the promoter region affects the initiation of transcription by preventing proper binding of RNA polymerase, leading to defective transcription initiation.

questions.stem: Klenow fragment lacks the activity of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 5'→3' Exonuclease

 

The Klenow fragment is a large fragment of DNA polymerase I that is formed after the removal of the 5'→3' exonuclease activity. This fragment retains both the 5'→3' polymerase activity and the 3'→5' exonuclease activity, which is responsible for proofreading. However, it lacks the 5'→3' exonuclease activity, which is used for primer removal.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 3'→5' Exonuclease: The Klenow fragment still retains its 3'→5' exonuclease activity, which is important for proofreading during DNA synthesis.

 

Option C. 5'→3' DNA polymerase: The Klenow fragment retains its 5'→3' polymerase activity, which is essential for synthesizing new DNA strands.

 

Option D. 3'→5' DNA polymerase: This is not a typical activity described for the Klenow fragment or any of the common polymerase enzymes, and hence, does not apply here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Klenow fragment lacks 5'→3' exonuclease activity but retains its 5'→3' polymerase and 3'→5' exonuclease proofreading activities.

questions.stem: Shine Dalgarno sequence in bacterial mRNA is near:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) AUG

 

The Shine-Dalgarno sequence is present near the AUG start codon in bacterial mRNA. This sequence helps in the initiation of protein synthesis by guiding the ribosome to the correct start codon (AUG), ensuring that translation begins at the appropriate site.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. UAA: UAA is a stop codon, which signals the termination of translation and is not involved in the Shine-Dalgarno sequence or the initiation of translation.

 

Option C. UAGGAGG: Although this sequence is part of the Shine-Dalgarno region, the question asks for the codon near it. AUG is the correct answer for the start codon.

 

Option D. UGA: UGA is another stop codon, used to terminate protein synthesis, not for the initiation process near the Shine-Dalgarno sequence.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Shine-Dalgarno sequence helps ribosomes locate the AUG start codon to initiate protein synthesis in bacterial mRNA.

questions.stem: Fidelity of protein translation depends upon:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Aminoacyl tRNA Synthetase

 

Fidelity of protein translation depends on the aminoacyl tRNA synthetase. This enzyme has proofreading activity, ensuring that the correct amino acid is attached to its corresponding tRNA. If a mistake occurs during this process, the resulting protein could be defective, as the wrong amino acid would be incorporated into the growing polypeptide chain.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. RNA Polymerase: RNA polymerase is involved in the transcription of RNA from DNA, but it does not directly affect the accuracy of protein translation.

 

Option B. DNA Polymerase: DNA polymerase is responsible for DNA replication, not protein translation.

 

Option C. mRNA Polymerase: There is no such enzyme specifically termed "mRNA Polymerase." The proper enzyme for mRNA synthesis is RNA polymerase.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Aminoacyl tRNA synthetase is responsible for ensuring the accuracy of amino acid incorporation during protein translation through its proofreading activity.

questions.stem: Which proofreading activity is critical in determining the accuracy of nuclear DNA replication?

options.label: A
options.text: 3’ to 5’ polymerase activity of DNA pol δ

options.label: B
options.text: 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity of DNA pol γ

options.label: C
options.text: 5’ to 3’ polymerase activity of DNA pol III

options.label: D
options.text: 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity of DNA pol δ

questions.answerText: 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity of DNA pol δ
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity of DNA pol δ

 

The proofreading activity critical for nuclear DNA replication is the 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity of DNA polymerase δ. This activity ensures the fidelity of DNA replication by allowing the polymerase to remove incorrectly incorporated nucleotides. DNA polymerase δ plays a crucial role in eukaryotic nuclear DNA replication, and its 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity helps maintain the accuracy of DNA synthesis by performing proofreading during replication.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 3’ to 5’ polymerase activity of DNA pol δ: This is not a known activity. DNA polymerase functions include polymerase activity and exonuclease activity, with the 3’ to 5’ exonuclease being the critical proofreading function.

 

Option B. 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity of DNA pol γ: DNA polymerase γ is responsible for mitochondrial DNA replication, not nuclear DNA replication. Thus, its proofreading activity does not influence nuclear DNA replication.

 

Option C. 5’ to 3’ polymerase activity of DNA pol III: This polymerase activity is important for prokaryotic DNA replication, but it does not have a role in the proofreading mechanism that maintains the fidelity of nuclear DNA replication in eukaryotes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The 3’ to 5’ exonuclease activity of DNA polymerase δ is essential for the proofreading and accuracy of nuclear DNA replication.

questions.stem: Primers are removed by all except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Beta polymerase

 

In eukaryotic cells, primers are removed by RNase H1 and FEN1, with delta polymerase also playing a role in replacing the primer with DNA. Beta polymerase, on the other hand, does not participate in primer removal. Instead, beta polymerase is involved in DNA repair processes and does not have the exonuclease activity required for primer removal.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Delta Polymerase: This polymerase is involved in the replacement of RNA primers with DNA during replication.

 

Option B. RNase H1: This enzyme removes RNA primers during DNA replication by cleaving the RNA strand of RNA-DNA hybrids.

 

Option C. FEN1: FEN1 (Flap Endonuclease 1) works in conjunction with RNase H1 and polymerase δ to remove RNA primers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Beta polymerase does not participate in primer removal; it is involved in DNA repair, unlike delta polymerase, RNase H1, and FEN1, which are active in the primer removal process.

questions.stem: Nitrogen atoms in purines are derived from all except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Glutamate

 

The nitrogen atoms in purines are derived from several sources. Aspartate contributes nitrogen to the purine ring at position 1, while glutamine provides nitrogen at positions 3 and 9. Glycine also plays a role in purine synthesis, contributing nitrogen atoms. However, glutamate is not directly involved in supplying nitrogen for the purine ring.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Aspartate: Aspartate provides a nitrogen atom to the purine ring at position 1.

 

Option B. Glutamine: Glutamine donates nitrogen to positions 3 and 9 in the purine ring.

 

Option D. Glycine: Glycine contributes nitrogen to the purine ring structure during synthesis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The nitrogen atoms in purines come from aspartate, glutamine, and glycine, but not from glutamate.

questions.stem: SYBR green dye is used in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Real-time PCR

 

SYBR green dye is used in real-time PCR (also known as quantitative PCR). It binds to double-stranded DNA and emits fluorescence. As PCR progresses and the amount of double-stranded DNA increases, the fluorescence intensity also increases. This allows for the real-time monitoring of DNA synthesis, helping quantify the amount of DNA being produced during the PCR process.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mass spectrometry: Mass spectrometry is a technique used for determining the molecular weight and structure of compounds but does not involve SYBR green dye.

 

Option C. RFLP detection: Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) is a technique used to analyze DNA fragments after enzyme digestion. It does not involve SYBR green dye.

 

Option D. FISH: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a technique used to detect specific DNA sequences in chromosomes, and it also does not use SYBR green dye.

 

Educational Objective:

 

SYBR green dye is specifically used in real-time PCR to bind to double-stranded DNA and allow for the quantification of DNA synthesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following codon does not show degeneracy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Methionine

 

Methionine does not show codon degeneracy. Degeneracy refers to the fact that multiple codons can code for the same amino acid. However, methionine is an exception because it is coded by only one codon, AUG. Therefore, methionine does not exhibit degeneracy, unlike other amino acids, such as serine, valine, and alanine, which are encoded by more than one codon.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Serine: Serine is encoded by multiple codons, showing degeneracy.

 

Option B. Valine: Valine also has multiple codons, demonstrating codon degeneracy.

 

Option C. Alanine: Alanine is encoded by more than one codon, showing degeneracy.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Methionine is unique in that it is encoded by a single codon, AUG, and does not display codon degeneracy.

Therefore, methionine does not exhibit degeneracy, unlike other amino acids, such as serine, valine, and alanine, which are encoded by more than one codon. Other Options: Option A. questions.stem: Which one of the following is a cofactor and not a coenzyme?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Copper

 

Copper is classified as a cofactor and not a coenzyme. A cofactor is typically a metal ion or inorganic molecule that assists enzymes in catalyzing reactions. Copper, being a metal ion, falls into this category. Unlike coenzymes, which are organic molecules, cofactors like copper do not act as independent carriers in enzymatic reactions but rather help in the enzyme's activity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Biotin: Biotin is an organic molecule and acts as a coenzyme in carboxylation reactions.

 

Option B. Tetrahydrofolic acid: Tetrahydrofolic acid is an organic molecule that serves as a coenzyme in one-carbon transfer reactions.

 

Option D. Pyridoxal phosphate: Pyridoxal phosphate is a coenzyme involved in amino acid metabolism and other enzymatic processes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Copper is a cofactor and not a coenzyme because it is a metal ion, while the other options are organic molecules acting as coenzymes.

questions.stem: A buffer that is most effective at pH of about 6.1 is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Bicarbonate Buffer

 

The bicarbonate buffer system is most effective at a pH of about 6.1. This is because the pKa of bicarbonate is around 6.1, making it most suitable for buffering in this pH range. It is widely used in physiological systems, especially in maintaining acid-base balance in blood.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acetate Buffer: Acetate buffer is most effective at a pH around 4.76, which is its pKa, and is not suitable for a pH of 6.1.

 

Option C. Phosphate Buffer: Phosphate buffer has an optimal buffering range closer to a pH of 7.2, making it less effective at pH 6.1.

 

Option D. Tris Buffer: Tris buffer is commonly used in laboratory settings but is most effective around a pH of 8.1, not 6.1.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The bicarbonate buffer is most effective at a pH of about 6.1 due to its pKa being closest to this value.

questions.stem: Which among the following serves as a cofactor for Glycogen phosphorylase:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Pyridoxal Phosphate

 

Pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6) serves as a cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase. Glycogen phosphorylase is the enzyme responsible for breaking down glycogen into glucose-1-phosphate. The enzyme requires pyridoxal phosphate to function properly, and its deficiency can impact glycogen breakdown, as seen in disorders like McArdle disease.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Thiamine: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) is involved in oxidative decarboxylation reactions, not glycogen breakdown.

 

Option B. Niacin: Niacin (Vitamin B3) functions in redox reactions in the form of NAD and NADP, not as a cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase.

 

Option D. Biotin: Biotin is a coenzyme for carboxylation reactions but is not involved with glycogen phosphorylase.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Pyridoxal phosphate (Vitamin B6) is the essential cofactor for glycogen phosphorylase, which is involved in glycogen breakdown.

questions.stem: Arsenic poisoning inhibits:

options.label: C
options.text: Branched chain alfa keto acid dehydrogenase

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) All of the above

 

Arsenic poisoning inhibits all three dehydrogenase complexes: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-keto-glutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase. This inhibition occurs because arsenite binds to lipoic acid, a cofactor essential for the activity of these enzyme complexes. Lipoic acid is necessary for the oxidative decarboxylation reactions catalyzed by these enzymes, and without it, the enzymes cannot function properly.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pyruvate dehydrogenase: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is inhibited by arsenite because it requires lipoic acid for its function.

 

Option B. Alpha-keto-glutarate dehydrogenase: This enzyme, involved in the Krebs cycle, is similarly inhibited due to the requirement for lipoic acid.

 

Option C. Branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase: This enzyme, important in the catabolism of branched-chain amino acids, is also inhibited by arsenite because it uses lipoic acid as a cofactor.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Arsenic inhibits multiple dehydrogenase enzymes by binding to lipoic acid, an essential cofactor for their activity.

questions.stem: In Vitamin C deficiency, post-translational modification of which amino acid is defective?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Lysine

 

In Vitamin C deficiency, the post-translational modification of proline to hydroxyproline and lysine to hydroxylysine is defective. Vitamin C is crucial for the hydroxylation of these amino acids, which is important in collagen synthesis. Without Vitamin C, collagen synthesis is impaired, leading to conditions like scurvy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Alanine: Alanine does not undergo post-translational modification dependent on Vitamin C.

 

Option C. Glycine: Glycine is not hydroxylated in a Vitamin C-dependent manner.

 

Option D. Arginine: Arginine is not modified by Vitamin C in post-translational processes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Vitamin C is required for the hydroxylation of lysine and proline during collagen synthesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following vitamins can act without phosphorylation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lipoamide

 

Lipoamide can act without phosphorylation. While other vitamins require phosphorylation to become active, such as pyridoxine (which is converted to pyridoxal phosphate) and thiamine (which becomes thiamine pyrophosphate), lipoamide functions directly as a cofactor for enzyme complexes without requiring a phosphate group for activation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pyridoxine: Pyridoxine is converted into its active form, pyridoxal phosphate, through phosphorylation.

 

Option C. Niacin: Niacin is converted to NAD/NADP, which involves phosphorylation as part of the activation process.

 

Option D. Thiamine: Thiamine requires phosphorylation to be converted into thiamine pyrophosphate, its active form.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lipoamide is a vitamin cofactor that does not require phosphorylation to function, unlike pyridoxine, niacin, and thiamine.

questions.stem: A lethal mutation occurs in a bacterium, rendering it incapable of replicating its chromosome. Because of this mutation, DNA synthesis produces many short fragments of DNA that have RNA sequences at their 5’ ends. The mutation is most likely in a gene encoding which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) DNA polymerase I

 

The bacterium’s inability to replicate its chromosome and the production of short DNA fragments with RNA sequences at their 5' ends suggest a problem with the removal of RNA primers during DNA synthesis. DNA polymerase I is responsible for removing RNA primers and replacing them with DNA during replication. If a mutation occurs in the gene encoding DNA polymerase I, the RNA primers will not be removed, leading to the accumulation of short DNA fragments with RNA at their 5' ends.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. DNA gyrase: DNA gyrase is involved in relieving torsional strain ahead of the replication fork but does not play a role in removing RNA primers.

 

Option B. DNA helicase: DNA helicase unwinds the DNA double helix during replication but does not remove RNA primers.

 

Option C. DNA ligase: DNA ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments but does not remove RNA primers.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A mutation in the gene encoding DNA polymerase I results in defective primer removal, leading to the accumulation of short DNA fragments with RNA sequences at their 5' ends.

questions.stem: Oligomer with a mutant base substitution is used in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Site-directed mutagenesis

 

An oligonucleotide with a mutant base substitution is used in site-directed mutagenesis. This technique involves introducing specific mutations at known sites to study the effects of the mutations on protein function or gene expression. The mutant oligonucleotide serves as a primer, allowing researchers to incorporate the desired mutation into the DNA sequence during replication.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. PCR: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is used for amplifying DNA, but it doesn't specifically involve introducing mutations with oligonucleotides.

 

Option C. DNA footprinting: DNA footprinting is used to study protein-DNA interactions and does not involve the introduction of base substitutions.

 

Option D. RFLP: Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP) is used to detect mutations by analyzing DNA fragment patterns but does not involve using an oligonucleotide with a mutant base substitution.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Site-directed mutagenesis involves the use of oligonucleotides with mutant base substitutions to introduce specific mutations into DNA for research purposes.

questions.stem: Cytosolic Cytochrome C mediates:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Apoptosis

 

When cytochrome C is released from the inner mitochondrial membrane into the cytosol, it no longer participates in the electron transport chain. Instead, it activates apoptosis. Cytosolic cytochrome C binds to apoptotic protease activating factor-1 (Apaf-1), leading to the formation of the apoptosome, which triggers the activation of caspases, resulting in programmed cell death (apoptosis).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Electron transport: Cytochrome C, when attached to the inner mitochondrial membrane, is involved in the electron transport chain. However, once it dissociates and enters the cytosol, it no longer functions in electron transport.

 

Option C. Krebs cycle: Cytochrome C does not play a direct role in the Krebs cycle, which occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.

 

Option D. Glycolysis: Cytochrome C is not involved in glycolysis, which takes place in the cytosol independently of mitochondrial functions.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cytosolic cytochrome C mediates apoptosis, not electron transport or other cellular processes.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company is studying a new antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis. When this antibiotic is added to an in vitro protein synthesis system that is translating the messenger RNA sequence AUGUUUUUUUAG, the only product formed is the dipeptide fMet-Phe. What step in protein synthesis is most likely inhibited by the antibiotic?

options.label: B
options.text: Binding of a charged transfer RNA to the ribosomal A site

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ribosomal translocation

 

If a dipeptide fMet-Phe is formed, it means that the processes of initiation and peptidyl transferase activity have occurred successfully, allowing the formation of the dipeptide. However, the fact that no further elongation occurs indicates that the ribosome is unable to move along the mRNA to the next codon, which suggests that ribosomal translocation is being inhibited by the antibiotic. Ribosomal translocation is the step where the ribosome moves from one codon to the next, and without this movement, protein synthesis halts after the dipeptide is formed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Initiation: Since the dipeptide is formed, initiation has already successfully occurred.

 

Option B. Binding of a charged transfer RNA to the ribosomal A site: Since the second amino acid (phenylalanine) is added to the growing peptide chain, binding to the A site must have happened.

 

Option C. Peptidyl transferase activity: Peptidyl transferase activity must be functional, as the dipeptide is successfully formed.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The inhibition of ribosomal translocation prevents further elongation, leading to the accumulation of dipeptides.

questions.stem: Digestive enzymes are:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Hydrolases


Digestive enzymes, such as amylase, lipase, and proteases, are classified as hydrolases. These enzymes catalyze the hydrolysis of various substrates, breaking down complex molecules like carbohydrates, proteins, and fats into simpler forms, facilitating digestion.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Oxidoreductases: These enzymes are involved in oxidation-reduction reactions, not digestion.


Option C. Dehydrogenases: Dehydrogenases are involved in catalyzing oxidation-reduction reactions, primarily during metabolic processes, but are not classified as digestive enzymes.


Option D. Ligases: Ligases are enzymes that catalyze the joining of two molecules, typically requiring energy from ATP, and are not involved in digestion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Digestive enzymes function as hydrolases, catalyzing the breakdown of complex molecules during digestion.

questions.stem: Tyrosinase is a:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Oxidase

 

Tyrosinase is an oxidase enzyme. It is involved in the oxidation of tyrosine to dopaquinone in melanin synthesis. Tyrosinase uses oxygen as an oxidizing agent, which is why it is classified as an oxidase.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Transferase: Transferases catalyze the transfer of functional groups between molecules, which is not the function of tyrosinase.

 

Option C. Lyase: Lyases break chemical bonds by means other than hydrolysis and oxidation, unlike tyrosinase, which functions as an oxidase.

 

Option D. Isomerase: Isomerases catalyze the rearrangement of atoms within a molecule, a role not played by tyrosinase.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tyrosinase is an oxidase enzyme that plays a key role in melanin biosynthesis.
